name: Colin Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, including anything different from your public answer. What is a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Colin, 58, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I worked at a parts counter before that business closed, and I'm still slower and less skilled at electrical work than the experienced crew. Today I sorted materials and helped fit parts under supervision, with the senior worker correcting a measurement I'd marked wrong. I like a task shown plainly and the feeling of getting the second try right; I don't like pretending I understood the first time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What should I know about home and your approach to new things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cleans houses part time, and our grown son and daughter live elsewhere. We rent our home, my pay is low, we've got about three weeks of expenses saved and there are few similar electrical jobs nearby. I never use AI tools and prefer a paper drawing and somebody I know showing me the work. I think about retirement, but I haven't got verified figures for what income we'd have or when; old employment papers still need sorting. I'd rather see a real wage, cost and task than argue about whether all change was good or bad.

I'd still ask for **practical checks** rather than try to look quicker than my current skill allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quieter future would do me. The office could tidy the invoices and I could keep learning the actual work. I'd still ask for a check instead of trying to look quicker than I was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about rent and ordinary bills with three weeks saved. The job could carry on just as it was and the wage would still be low. Being closer to retirement doesn't make the next rent payment smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd buy one newspaper a week instead of a daily copy and use the difference for bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep the supervised preparation and fitting work with the familiar paper notes. I'd ask my daughter whether she could help find the right place to request official retirement information, without assuming she could pay our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with relief that the work wasn't changing quickly. I'd still be embarrassed by a mistake, but that wasn't the same as needing to invent a whole new job tomorrow. I'd want the pay to keep coming while I learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would changing the newspaper purchase achieve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the weekly paper I actually had time to read. It's a small cut, not a way to replace a wage. I'd put it towards bills rather than claim I'd started a new retirement fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your daughter to provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help finding and reading the right records, not an instruction to send us money. My daughter keeps family documents organised, but she has her own bills. I'd ask whether she had time before treating the help as arranged.

I'd want **paid instruction** for a real new requirement rather than a neat schedule that hid the learning gap.
think: My **hours could shrink** if planning changes squeeze the paid time given to slower beginners.
Former **counter experience** might support a job application, without protecting that work from thinking-task automation.
do: Keep the **current wage** and require paid instruction before accepting any role needing unfamiliar software.
Apply for posted **parts-counter work** during the first year only where duties fit actual ability.
Leave only for signed **fixed hours and pay** covering essentials after travel, while retaining the newspaper cut.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, while able to examine actual adverts and ask for instruction without claiming new skills.

fieldNote: His **job search** uses actual applications and former counter experience, without upgrading his present junior electrical skill or claiming permanent automation shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office could use a quicker system without expecting a beginner's hands to learn at the same speed. I'd ask the supervisor what paid teaching came with any new requirement. I wouldn't want a neat schedule to hide the checks I still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical tasks would still exist, but I could lose hours if quicker planning left less paid time for a slower beginner. I'd have little room to wait for that to sort itself out. My old counter experience might give me something familiar to apply for, without making that job safe from software either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for clear paid hours and supervision at the work review, keeping the current wage while I checked actual posted parts-counter vacancies. In the first year I'd apply to those with duties I could actually do. I'd leave only for signed fixed hours and pay that covered essential bills after travel, and keep the newspaper cut meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid hours, and not keen on learning another screen just to keep the same money. I could still read an advert and ask a plain question. I'd prefer a familiar task with a real wage to a grand promise about retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a parts-counter job avoid the same technology changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, ordering parts, checking stock and answering customers are thinking tasks too. I'd want the actual paid duties and terms, not a story that my former job was protected forever. A counter job could provide my next wage without being safe from thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a vacancy required unfamiliar software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask who would teach it during paid time before accepting the role. I wouldn't claim I could use an unfamiliar system to secure the offer. I'd compare a real requirement with what I could actually do.

fieldNote: His **alarm** follows expected major wage loss and sleeplessness, without assuming age 63 provides a pension or affordable exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 when I'd be 60, and capable robots follow around 2031 when I'd be 63. I'd ask what paid work was actually planned. I'd also check the old employment records instead of assuming being near retirement took care of the second date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a large share of my junior hours to go as firms prepared for capable hands-on machines. Counter work could be squeezed earlier by thinking AI, so I couldn't just promise to go back there. Three weeks saved would not bridge the income gap, and I'd be awake wondering what the old papers actually added up to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my daughter for help obtaining official retirement information and locating free community advice, checking availability instead of assuming an appointment. We'd compare confirmed figures with the actual rent and essentials, counting no pension, support or family payment before it was verified and agreed. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep suitable supervised paid work while available and keep buying only the weekly newspaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large wage loss, even though I could still ask for help and sort the papers. I'd want someone to listen without assuming I could just retire. An age in a record doesn't tell me what reaches the rent account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What questions would you take to the advice service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what income, if any, was actually payable, when it could start and what conditions applied. I'd want any support explained as a payment or loan with its costs. I wouldn't count a requested record or submitted form as money already approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no immediate advice appointment was available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask another actual community service about availability and keep the current suitable paid work where possible. I wouldn't tell my daughter that finding my papers made her responsible for the gap. Asking for help should still leave room for an honest no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check real resources before promising a different working life. I'd be 63 when thinking work changed in 2031 and about 66 when robots followed around 2034. I'd still ask about paid teaching for the work I needed to do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have more time to improve at supervised tasks and understand the retirement records. But low pay, rent and three weeks of savings would still be our position today. I can't assume another three birthdays would produce income I haven't checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my daughter to help obtain official records and keep suitable supervised paid work while it was available. In the first year after 2031 we'd compare verified income with essentials; if I still needed wages, I'd apply for posted parts-counter jobs only where duties fitted my actual ability. I'd leave the current job only for signed fixed hours and pay covering essential bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, with less urgency around the next decision. I'd hope the extra time let us check a real option carefully. I wouldn't describe a possible future exit as one we'd already funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about a counter vacancy at those ages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the real duties and hours rather than assume I could do any job because I needed it. Counter work would still face thinking AI too. I'd want a genuine paid opportunity, not an argument that an old title was safe.

transcript.text: Would you count on the grown children paying towards the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask for record help and a conversation before counting anything. They have their own households and needs. I'd rather know what our verified resources were before asking anyone else about a particular gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to find the actual figures instead of calling every older worker retired. I'd be 68 when thinking work changed in 2036 and about 71 when robots followed around 2039. I'd still want paid work to remain understandable and checked while I needed it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might want to have stopped by those dates, but I don't know a verified income that would let us. I also can't assume I'd be able to do physical electrical work or find another job at 68. Today's low wage and short reserve would still leave me anxious while I checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my daughter for help obtaining official income records and keep suitable supervised paid work while available. In the first year after 2036 we'd compare confirmed income, essentials and actual work capacity before any exit decision. If I still needed a wage and could do the duties, I'd apply for posted counter roles, changing only for signed fixed hours and pay covering essentials after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our present money, though less hurried by the distant robot date. I'd want a choice grounded in real resources. I wouldn't write a pension into the budget because a birthday sounded old enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your age alone tell you whether to stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd need actual figures for rent, food, other essentials and any confirmed income then. My partner's ability to keep working wouldn't be guaranteed either. I'd ask those questions before saying we could stop or must carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the grown children contribute to the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only help they had actually chosen and we had agreed, not wages I imagined because they were grown. I'd ask for help reading the records first. Their own bills don't disappear when mine become difficult.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large junior-wage loss without a checked retirement income ready to replace it. Paid practical instruction for actual tasks and help obtaining the official income records would help. I'd like the real figures before someone tells me I'm nearly finished working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether an older person can be new at the job without everyone assuming a lifetime of electrical skill. I have a vocational certificate and still need someone to check my work. My birthdate doesn't sign off a circuit or pay the rent.
